newsitem.title: USA: APL says no decision yet on shipping alliances.
newsitem.headline: APL says no decision yet on shipping alliances.

text.p: The planned merger between shipping giants APL Ltd and Neptune Orient Lines Ltd will eventually force a realignment of two key shipping alliances, but no decision would be taken until after the merger is completed, APL said on Tuesday.

"The merged NOL-APL will continue to operate within alliances and we don't forsee splitting our fleet among more than one major alliance within a particular trade route," said APL spokesman Gil Roeder.
"Our desire is to stay within the Global Alliance," he added. "However, the fact that NOL is presently in the Grand Alliance is an issue that needs to be resolved among the parties."

The future of APL's participation in the five-member Global Alliance was thrown into doubt on Tuesday after another of its members, Dutch Royal Nedlloyd, announced it would be jumping ship to join the rival Grand Alliance, in which its newly-merged corporate partner, Britain's P&O Containers, is already a member.
P&O and Nedlloyd have been operating in the opposing alliances since their merger went into effect on January 1.
The Global and the Grand Alliance are two of some 20 legalized shipping cartels worldwide that share vessels and terminals and establish freight rates on major trading routes.

P&O Nedlloyd's decision to abandon the Global partnership leaves it with four members: APL, Japan's Mitsui OSK Lines, Malaysian International Shipping Corp and Hong Kong's Orient Overseas Container Lines (OOCL).
Along with P&O Nedlloyd, the Grand Alliance includes Germany's Hapag Lloyd and Japan's Nipon Yusen Kaisha (NYK).
The remaining members of the Global Alliance on Tuesday issued a statement saying Nedlloyd's departure had been expected and that its service network would not be affected by the switch.
But the group said the details of next year's deployment were still under discussion and that the future of its long-term service structure would be announced "in due course."

In April, Singapore-based NOL announced its plan to acquire APL, the second-biggest carrier in the U.S. after Sea-Land Service Inc, in a deal valued at more than $800 million. The combined company will operate a fleet of 113 ships, including 76 container vessels.
APL's Roeder said no announcement on the alliances would be forthcoming until its takeover by Neptune is completed sometime in the fall. A spokesman for NOL in London also declined further comment.
While the merged APL-NOL could elect to join either cartel, analysts said P&O Nedlloyd's adherence to the Grand Alliance could tilt the scales in favor of APL-NOL membership in that group.

"The more an alliance can consolidate capacity, the more likely it is that the alliance will be successful," said one analyst who requested anonymity. "The bigger the alliance is, the more benefits you can get from it."

APL, formerly called American President Cos, also participates in a trans-Pacific alliance with Matson Navigation and has formed a joint shipping venture with Mexican firm Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM).
